analysis.one_liner: Cuts the tax on investment gains roughly in half, adjusts asset values for inflation, and lets home sellers deduct losses.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced in January 1994 and died there when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let every taxpayer deduct half of their capital gains from taxable income, cutting the tax on profits from selling stocks and business assets roughly in half. It would also have raised the 'cost basis' of stocks and business property held more than a year to account for inflation, shrinking taxable gains further. And it would have created a new deduction for people who sell their home for less than they paid for it.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who realize capital gains — profits from selling stocks, business property, and similar assets. Those gains are concentrated in the wealthiest households, so the largest dollar benefits flow to high-income investors, though moderate-income savers with mutual funds or appreciated assets would also pay less. A separate provision would help homeowners who sell at a loss.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Stock and business-asset investors, mostly wealthy

how_it_helps.text: Allows a 50 percent income tax deduction for net capital gains for both corporate and noncorporate taxpayers.

Requires indexing of the tax basis of corporate stock and tangible business property held more than one year, using the gross national product deflator, so gains caused purely by inflation would not be taxed.
The bill's conforming provisions set the effective tax rate on gains at roughly 17.5 to 19.8 percent, down from the 28 to 35 percent rates then in effect for withholding and related calculations.
Allows an itemized deduction for losses from the sale or exchange of a principal residence, a benefit to homeowners who sell in a falling market.

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenue would fall, since the bill contains no offsetting tax increases or spending cuts. The lost revenue would be made up by other taxpayers, by cutting spending, or by borrowing. Because most taxable capital gains are realized by the highest-income households, the practical effect would be to shift tax burden away from investment income and toward wages.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the 50 percent exclusion for gains on certain small-business stock created by the 1993 Revenue Reconciliation Act, consolidating that benefit into the general capital gains deduction.
The bill contains no offsetting revenue provisions, so the full cost of the capital gains deduction and indexing would add to the deficit or require higher taxes elsewhere.

Inflation indexing applies only to a defined set of assets and excludes creditor interests, options, net lease property, preferred stock, and most foreign and S corporation stock, creating complexity and line-drawing disputes for taxpayers and the IRS.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The housing loss deduction is a genuine, narrow help to ordinary homeowners caught in declining markets. But the bill's centerpiece — the 50 percent gains deduction plus inflation indexing — delivers by far its largest dollar benefits to households with the biggest investment portfolios, while cutting federal revenue with no offsets. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that this is a large tax cut skewed toward the top, sold as a jobs measure, and that the jobs connection is indirect at best.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Bill Archer introduced the bill on January 26, 1994, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
53 representatives signed on as cosponsors — 42 Republicans and 11 Democrats.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a subcommittee or committee markup, never reached the House floor, and died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, capital gains were taxed at existing rates and federal revenue was untouched. Ordinary taxpayers who would have shouldered the cost of a large tax cut on investment gains were spared it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary taxpayers and the federal treasury

for.name: Rep. Bill Archer
for.role: Sponsor; senior Republican on the Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 11 colleagues to join as original cosponsors.

for.name: 11 of 258 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a small bipartisan footprint.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; after its referral on the day of introduction, the committee took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's backing was heavily Republican — 42 of 53 cosponsors — though 11 Democrats signed on, and it died in a committee controlled by Democrats without any vote ever being held.

industries.industry: Capital gains investors (concentrated in the wealthiest households)
industries.note: The 50 percent deduction and inflation indexing would have cut the tax rate on investment gains roughly in half, with the largest dollar benefits going to those with the biggest portfolios. The revenue cost would fall on everyone else through deficits or higher taxes elsewhere.

industries.industry: Mutual funds, REITs, and the securities industry
industries.note: The bill includes detailed pass-through rules letting regulated investment companies and real estate investment trusts apply inflation indexing at the entity level, and lower taxes on gains would encourage more investment through these vehicles. Smaller savers holding fund shares would also pay less tax on their gains.

Homeowners selling at a loss would gain a new deduction, and owners of business real estate would get inflation indexing. The home-loss provision is the piece of the bill that most directly serves ordinary people.
